lead.headline: Putin's United Russia claims record Duma supermajority in wartime vote
lead.dek: Preliminary results give the Kremlin's ruling party 355 of 450 seats after a three-day election held with anti-war parties excluded and under a barrage of Ukrainian drones.
body: President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party won 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, Russia's lower house of parliament, according to preliminary results released on Monday by election chief Ella Pamfilova. The total beats the party's previous high of 343 seats from 2016 and hands it a supermajority. Pamfilova said more than 95 per cent of ballots had been counted and put turnout at just over 59 per cent, with final figures due later in the week.

The Communist Party came a distant second with 40 seats, followed by the nationalist LDPR with 25 and New People with 20. Early party-list tallies reported by TASS had United Russia at close to 58 per cent of the vote. More than 3.6 million people voted online, and ballots were also cast in Crimea and four Ukrainian regions Moscow claims to have annexed, which the UN and most countries do not recognise as Russian.

The vote, held from 18 to 20 September, was the first parliamentary election since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. No party critical of Putin took part. Yabloko, the only registered party openly opposed to the war, was struck off by the Supreme Court in August, and its leader Nikolai Rybakov spoiled his own ballot with a message calling for peace.

Ukraine called the election illegitimate, especially in occupied territory. Moscow accused Kyiv of trying to disrupt the vote after a huge wave of drone attacks on Sunday that TASS described as the biggest of the war. Al Jazeera, citing Russian officials, reported three deaths in the Moscow region, two in Russian-held Kherson including an election official, and damage at a Moscow oil refinery.

Analysts at the Berlin-based think tank NEST suggested some votes for the Communists and New People could be quiet protest against economic strain. With a supermajority secured, the Kremlin faces no parliamentary obstacle as it continues the war, now well into its fifth year.
lead.why: The result locks in Kremlin control of Russia's legislature for the coming years, leaving no domestic institutional check on the war in Ukraine.

more.headline: Merz's CDU suffers historic defeats in two German state elections
more.dek: The chancellor's party collapsed in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and lost Berlin to the Left, while the far-right AfD surged.
body: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats suffered heavy losses in state elections on Sunday. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU fell to about 4.9 per cent, below the 5 per cent threshold, while the far-right AfD came first with 38.2 per cent, ahead of the Social Democrats on 35.5 per cent. In Berlin, the Left party won with 25.7 per cent, the CDU dropped to 18.8 per cent from 28.2 per cent in 2023, and the AfD rose to 16.3 per cent.

Merz, 70 and in office for 16 months, called the outcome a disaster but said he would stay on as party leader and chancellor until the end of his term, insisting his economic reforms must go ahead. He cancelled a planned trip to the UN General Assembly. Despite its gains, the AfD has no realistic path into government in either state because other parties refuse to work with it.
more.why: Weakness at the top of Europe's largest economy, and a strengthening far right, affect EU policy on Ukraine, migration and economic reform.

more.headline: US readies sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court itself
more.dek: Washington is preparing to sanction the court as an institution, a step that could hobble its finances and daily operations.
body: The Trump administration has prepared sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court as a whole and plans to announce them soon, two sources told Reuters, following a report in the Wall Street Journal. The measures would bar US citizens and companies from providing money, goods or services to the court without a Treasury licence, after a grace period of six to seven months. Until now, the US has sanctioned more than a dozen individual ICC judges and prosecutors, but never the institution.

ICC leaders have warned that court-wide sanctions could disrupt IT and insurance contracts, the hiring of investigators and routine payments, including salaries for American staff. Washington, which has never joined the court, objects to its arrest warrants for Israeli leaders and a past investigation involving US personnel in Afghanistan. Secretary of State Marco Rubio launched a campaign in July urging countries to quit the court.
more.why: Sanctioning the world's permanent war crimes court as an institution could cripple international accountability for genocide and war crimes.

lead.headline: Trump threatens to annihilate Iran in combative UN speech
lead.dek: At the UN General Assembly, the US president demanded Iran's economic isolation and predicted a deal only after November's midterms, as Iran's delegation walked out.
body: US President Donald Trump used his address to the 81st UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday to defend the war with Iran and again threaten the Islamic Republic with destruction. He framed his choice as one between a deal and moving to wipe out the Iranian state quickly, and he called for the complete economic isolation of Iran. Members of Iran's delegation walked out while he spoke.

Trump accused Tehran of stalling on a deal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz until after the US midterm elections in November. He predicted an agreement would come shortly after the vote, while insisting the election played no part in his own thinking. He also repeated that he would never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.

The war began on 28 February, when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran. A memorandum of understanding signed in June collapsed within weeks after Iran resumed attacks on tankers, and US strikes restarted. The US now blockades Iranian ports and escorts commercial ships. Before the war, about a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments passed through Hormuz; National Review reported that US gasoline prices have risen by nearly half since the conflict began.

Hours before the speech, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran could reopen the strait within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted the blockade. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said Trump could not impose his will on Iranians. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US remained open to talks that could produce results.

After the speech, Trump met Gulf leaders from Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, who want shipping restored but are wary of empowering Iran. Qatar has floated a regional security framework that Iran is said to be reviewing.
lead.why: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most important energy chokepoint, so the war's direction drives fuel prices and inflation around the globe.

more.headline: Sri Lanka convicts 15 men over 2019 Easter Sunday bombings
more.dek: After a trial lasting more than five years, a Colombo court found 15 men guilty of roles in attacks that killed more than 260 people.
body: A court in Colombo on Tuesday convicted 15 men for their part in organising the April 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, in which suicide attackers struck three churches and three luxury hotels. The attacks, inspired by the Islamic State group and blamed on two local militant groups, killed more than 260 people, including 42 foreigners, and wounded around 500. The men were sentenced to life in prison; Sri Lanka has not carried out an execution since 1976.

Charges were filed in 2021 against 24 suspects, covering murder, terrorism conspiracy and weapons offences. None of the bombers survived. In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence official were sentenced to death for ignoring foreign intelligence warnings. Sri Lanka's Catholic Church maintains, without offering evidence, that the true masterminds have not been identified.
more.why: The verdicts are a milestone in one of South Asia's deadliest terror attacks, which shook Sri Lanka's tourism economy and its religious communities.

more.headline: Typhoon Dujuan kills at least four around Tokyo
more.dek: Record rainfall triggered landslides and left tens of thousands of homes without power in Chiba as the storm swept past the Japanese capital.
body: Typhoon Dujuan killed at least four people in the Tokyo region, three in Chiba prefecture and one in Kanagawa, according to Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency. Six people were missing and 22 injured after torrential rain set off landslides. More than 45,000 households in Chiba were still without electricity on Tuesday afternoon, and over 460 homes were damaged.

NHK reported 832mm of rain over 48 hours on Oshima island, more than twice its usual September total, while Tokyo's Edogawa ward set a 24-hour record of 282.5mm. The storm disrupted trains and roads and forced a major video game fair in Tokyo to close early before moving out over the Pacific.
more.why: Extreme rainfall hitting one of the world's largest metropolitan areas shows how intensifying storms test even well-prepared cities.

lead.headline: Iran's Pezeshkian defies Trump at UN but keeps door to talks open
lead.dek: A day after Trump's threats, Iran's president told world leaders his country was a victim of terrorism, as US envoys and Iranian officials held their first contact in weeks.
body: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that Iran had been the victim of terrorism, not its sponsor, responding directly to Donald Trump's threats the day before. He held up photos of children killed when a missile hit a school in Minab on the first day of the war, a strike that killed 156 people, and an image of the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, killed in the opening attacks. The US delegation walked out.

Pezeshkian said Iran wanted military strength only for self-defence, rejected the idea that nuclear knowledge should belong to a few nations, and said the dispute had no military solution. He said Iran would not surrender its navigation rights in the Strait of Hormuz. He ended by saying Tehran was ready for negotiations, though not under threat of force.

Behind the speeches, diplomacy stirred. On Tuesday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held about three hours of talks with an Iranian team led by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, with Qatar mediating. Witkoff called the round constructive and promising, and Iranian state media described it as the first direct contact in weeks. Iran's conditions include lifting the US naval blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending the war on all fronts.

Reactions were guarded. Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed Pezeshkian's human rights claims and warned against calling the talks a breakthrough. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said the meeting produced nothing new. Iran's military warned of crushing blows if attacked again.

Euronews noted that Pezeshkian's claim that Iran had not targeted civilians is contradicted by documented deaths of sailors and civilians in Iranian attacks across the region. Qatar and Pakistan are continuing mediation efforts.
lead.why: Any opening between Washington and Tehran could decide whether the Hormuz shipping crisis eases or the war escalates again, with global energy markets in the balance.

more.headline: Tigray leaders declare new war as Ethiopia peace deal crumbles
more.dek: Tigrayan forces seized airports and fought in neighbouring Afar and Amhara, threatening the 2022 Pretoria Agreement.
body: Leaders in Ethiopia's Tigray region said on Wednesday they had entered a new war with the federal government, describing it as defensive, as fighting broke out in Tigray and the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said Tigrayan forces had taken federally held airports and launched an all-out offensive. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to the region. Days earlier, the TPLF had announced an alliance with six other armed groups aiming to topple Abiy.

The 2020 to 2022 Tigray war killed hundreds of thousands of people before the Pretoria Agreement. The government accuses Eritrea of funding the alliance, which Eritrea has denied. The African Union called for immediate de-escalation, and the US ambassador called the offensive an unwinnable fight.
more.why: A renewed war in Africa's second most populous country could pull in Eritrea and destabilise the entire Horn of Africa.

more.headline: Hurricane Polo becomes one of the strongest Pacific storms on record
more.dek: The Category 5 hurricane reached 180mph winds off Mexico's southwest coast, forcing port closures in Guerrero and Michoacan.
body: Hurricane Polo strengthened into a Category 5 storm with maximum sustained winds of 180mph (290km/h) off Mexico's Pacific coast, the US National Hurricane Center said, citing a NOAA Hurricane Hunter flight. Colorado State University's Phil Klotzbach said it tied the strongest Northern Hemisphere storms of 2026 and ranked second by pressure among recorded eastern Pacific systems, behind 2015's Hurricane Patricia. It was the season's third Category 5 Pacific hurricane.

Forecasters expected the compact storm to stay offshore and turn northwest, but warned of heavy rain, dangerous surf and mudslides. Mexico's navy closed ports in Guerrero and Michoacan, and President Claudia Sheinbaum urged coastal residents to stay alert.
more.why: The rapid intensification of Pacific hurricanes is a growing risk for coastal communities and ports along Mexico's busy Pacific shipping routes.

lead.headline: Trump hosts Xi at White House, extends trade truce to January
lead.dek: Xi's first Washington visit in more than a decade brought lavish ceremony, a two-month trade extension and sharp differences on Taiwan and AI.
body: President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday for a state visit, Xi's first trip to Washington in over a decade. The programme included a red-carpet arrival at Joint Base Andrews, a Rose Garden ceremony with a military flyover and a state dinner whose guests reportedly included Tim Cook, Sundar Pichai, Sam Altman and Jensen Huang.

The main concrete outcome was on trade. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides agreed to extend their trade truce, which was due to lapse in November, by two months to 10 January. Xi said a new trade arrangement had been reached and called it good news for the global economy. Bessent said China had met its pledge to buy 25 million tonnes of soybeans but lagged on other farm purchases, while rare-earth deliveries were also falling short.

On Taiwan, Chinese state media said Xi urged Washington to handle the issue with prudence and to oppose Taiwanese independence, a stronger stance than the long-standing US position of not supporting it. The White House issued no immediate readout. Xi also called for regular military dialogue and better crisis-prevention tools.

The leaders diverged on artificial intelligence. Xi said both countries had a responsibility to keep AI under human control, while Trump posted that he wanted to leave the technology largely where it is, without new guardrails. They also discussed the Korean peninsula, the Middle East and the war in Ukraine; Xinhua said Xi backed a return to a US-Iran ceasefire.

US television networks did not carry the leaders' remarks live in protest at the White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again at APEC in Shenzhen and the G20 in Miami.
lead.why: Relations between the world's two largest economies shape global trade, technology supply chains and security in the Taiwan Strait.

more.headline: Delegates walk out as Netanyahu defends Israel at the UN
more.dek: Dozens left the General Assembly hall as Israel's prime minister called genocide accusations the biggest lie of the century.
body: Dozens of delegates walked out of the UN General Assembly on Thursday as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to the podium, following a Palestinian appeal for a collective walkout. Netanyahu mocked those leaving and rejected genocide allegations over Gaza. He also described the decision to attack Iran as one of the easiest he had made and said some leaders privately thanked Israel for it.

He attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who had called him a war criminal. Earlier that day, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the assembly by recorded video after the US refused him a visa for the second year running, calling for urgent progress towards a two-state solution.
more.why: The walkout showed Israel's deepening diplomatic isolation over Gaza and the Iran war, even as it keeps strong US backing.

more.headline: Late Gakpo equaliser spoils Klopp's first game as Germany coach
more.dek: The Netherlands drew 1-1 with Germany in Amsterdam in a Nations League opener that also featured new Dutch coach Xavi.
body: Jurgen Klopp's reign as Germany coach began with a 1-1 draw against the Netherlands in Amsterdam on Thursday in the opening round of the UEFA Nations League. Felix Nmecha put Germany ahead from close range in the 32nd minute, but Cody Gakpo equalised in stoppage time from a cross by debutant Ruben van Bommel.

Germany lost Jamal Musiala to injury in the warm-up and Kai Havertz also limped off. Klopp told broadcaster RTL that plenty had gone well, while admitting his side struggled for a spell after a strong start. The Netherlands are now coached by former Barcelona and Spain midfielder Xavi Hernandez, who succeeded Ronald Koeman.
more.why: Klopp, one of the world's best-known managers, has been tasked with rebuilding a four-time world champion national team.

lead.headline: Iran offers seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
lead.dek: Tehran says it would reopen the vital waterway and restart nuclear talks within a week if the US lifts its blockade, waives oil sanctions and agrees a wider ceasefire.
body: Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear negotiations within seven days if the United States meets a set of conditions, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. He outlined the plan at a private gathering in New York on Thursday, and it was widely reported on Friday. The proposal was passed to Washington through mediators, with Qatar relaying messages.

According to the AP, Iran's terms are that the US lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observe a ceasefire that includes Lebanon. Al Jazeera reported that the clock would start the day after the US accepts, with the strait reopening at the end of the seventh day and talks resuming after that.

The plan closely resembles the memorandum of understanding signed on 17 June, which set a 60-day window of toll-free shipping and negotiations before collapsing amid renewed attacks. Iran's new version speeds up the timeline and changes the order of steps. Araghchi described his meeting earlier in the week with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as productive.

Washington was cautious. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US wants Iran's nuclear programme dealt with immediately as part of one package and warned against calling recent contacts a breakthrough. Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute, who attended the gathering, said Araghchi pitched a fast deal as helpful to Trump before the midterms, while noting suspicion that Iran might be buying time to sell more oil.

Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera doubted Washington would revive the June framework, arguing the US believes it can outlast Iran economically. Pezeshkian hosted Qatar's prime minister early on Friday as mediation continued.
lead.why: Reopening Hormuz would ease a squeeze on global oil and gas supplies that has fuelled inflation worldwide for seven months.

more.headline: US Supreme Court again blocks Missouri's redrawn congressional map
more.dek: For the third time, the justices refused to let Missouri use a 2025 map designed to win Republicans an extra House seat in November.
body: The US Supreme Court on Friday paused an appeals court ruling that would have required Missouri to use a congressional map drawn in 2025, meaning the state's 2022 districts will be used in November's midterm elections. The unsigned order, with no public dissents, said switching maps after the election had begun would cause chaos. It was the third time the court had intervened.

The new map aimed to give Republicans seven of Missouri's eight House seats by carving up Democrat Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City district. Missouri's Supreme Court ruled that a citizen referendum petition with more than 300,000 signatures blocks the map unless voters approve it. Governor Mike Kehoe called the decision disappointing; Cleaver welcomed it.
more.why: Mid-decade redistricting battles could decide which party controls the US House, shaping Washington's policy on trade, Iran and Ukraine.

more.headline: Anthropic signs $11.6bn seven-year cloud deal with Akamai
more.dek: The AI company's commitment could grow to about $20bn and comes with a warrant for up to 5% of Akamai's stock.
body: Akamai Technologies said Anthropic has committed $11.6bn over seven years to use its cloud computing services, with an option for up to $9bn more. Akamai also issued Anthropic a warrant for about 7.7 million shares, roughly 5% of its stock, at $111.33 each. About 2% vests with the initial commitment and the rest as spending expands. Akamai shares jumped as much as 17% in late trading after the announcement.

CEO Tom Leighton said it was the first time Akamai had granted a warrant in a customer deal. According to Bloomberg, Akamai expects to spend about $5.5bn in capital to serve the contract, which is due to start in the second half of 2027. Some investors have voiced concern about circular AI deals.
more.why: The deal shows the vast sums AI developers are committing to computing capacity, reshaping the global cloud industry.

lead.headline: Trump rejects Iran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
lead.dek: Calling the seven-day offer unacceptable, Trump said Iran wanted a quick deal because it was losing badly, dimming hopes of an early end to the war.
body: President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, telling reporters outside the White House it would not be acceptable. He said Tehran wanted an immediate opening because it was losing badly. Early that morning he had posted an image on Truth Social labelling the waterway the Trump Strait.

Under the plan set out by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Iran would restore normal shipping within a week if the US lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waived sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observed a ceasefire covering Lebanon. Araghchi said Iran wanted nothing beyond the terms of the June memorandum of understanding and that the choice now lay with Washington.

The rejection followed a week of diplomacy at the UN, including three hours of indirect talks on 22 September, the first such round since the June deal collapsed. A White House official described talks through mediators as positive and constructive but said the US was in a strong position and in no hurry. Rubio said any deal would require a lot of hard work over time.

The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that Trump had told aides a renewed bombing campaign was likely after the midterms, though officials said that could change. For Iran, lifting the blockade and sanctions would relieve an economy suffering record-low currency values and soaring inflation. For the US, reopening the strait would calm markets and reduce the burden on naval forces escorting ships.

Analyst Danny Citrinowicz of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies said Washington may believe time is on its side, while Tehran may conclude the opposite. Pezeshkian has returned to Tehran, according to Iranian media.
lead.why: The rejection prolongs the closure of a chokepoint for about a fifth of global oil and gas trade and raises the risk of renewed strikes.

more.headline: All of Bangkok declared a disaster zone after days of rain
more.dek: Nearly 300mm of rain flooded roads and homes across the Thai capital, prompting a disaster declaration in all 50 districts.
body: Bangkok authorities declared all 50 of the city's districts disaster zones on Saturday after almost 300mm of rain fell from Thursday afternoon, flooding roads, homes and shops. Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said canals were full and warned residents near them, while about 980 people moved into temporary shelters. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul cut short a trip to London.

The city said pumping stations were at full capacity and draining could take two to three days once the rain stopped. Bangkok had recorded 487mm of rain from 1 to 25 September, against an average of about 269mm. One canalside vendor told reporters the flooding was worse than in 2011, when nationwide floods killed more than 500 people.
more.why: Flooding in a low-lying megacity of millions shows the growing climate risk to Asia's economic hubs and supply chains.

more.headline: Pope Leo draws huge crowd to open-air Mass in Paris
more.dek: Hundreds of thousands filled the Champs-Elysees and Place de la Concorde on the first official papal visit to France in nearly two decades.
body: Pope Leo XIV celebrated an open-air Mass at the Place de la Concorde in Paris on Saturday after travelling down the Champs-Elysees in his popemobile. Vatican crowd estimates were reported at between about 700,000 (AFP) and 800,000 (AP). Central Paris was closed to traffic. The four-day trip began on Friday with prayers at the restored Notre Dame, the first papal visit since the 2019 fire, and a youth vigil.

In his homily, Leo urged believers to share their faith. During the visit he also warned against an AI-driven paradise of machines and called on France to champion peace. Adult baptisms in France have roughly tripled since 2016, though overall numbers remain far below past levels. The pope travelled on to Lourdes.
more.why: The first US-born pope is using major foreign visits to push the Church's message on AI ethics, migration and peace.

lead.headline: Two mass shootings in South African townships kill at least 27
lead.dek: Gunmen attacked a tavern near Johannesburg and a store near Cape Town within hours of each other, in one of the country's deadliest weekends of gun violence.
body: At least 27 people were killed and more than 20 wounded in two mass shootings in separate South African townships, police said on Sunday. A day later, the toll rose to 28 when another victim died in hospital. No arrests had been announced in either case.

The first attack happened at about 9:30pm on Saturday at a tavern in Wedela, southwest of Johannesburg. Police said eight gunmen armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols shot at people outside and then inside, killing 17 people and wounding 15. The attackers searched some customers and took their phones before fleeing in two vehicles, and two cars were set on fire outside. About four hours later, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 at a store linked to an entertainment venue in Lwandle, near Cape Town.

Soldiers were sent to Wedela on Sunday, and detectives and specialist units were assigned to both cases. A resident told the AP that earlier local shootings had involved illegal mining gangs but nothing on this scale. Police have opened 17 murder cases and 15 attempted murder cases for Wedela alone.

The attacks came five days after gunmen killed at least 11 people, including a pregnant woman, at a house party in KwaMakhutha near Durban. Police statistics show 5,427 murders in the three months to 30 June, about 60 a day, with shootings the most common cause. Political parties and gun owners estimate that between 2 million and 6 million illegal firearms are circulating.

In March, President Cyril Ramaphosa deployed soldiers to help police in a year-long anti-crime operation in high-crime areas, calling gang crime the biggest threat to South Africa's democracy and economy. The latest killings will add pressure on the government to show results.
lead.why: South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, and gang violence threatens investment and stability in Africa's most industrialised economy.

more.headline: Serbia's Vucic resigns as president to run for prime minister
more.dek: Aleksandar Vucic stepped down months before his term ends, ahead of a snap parliamentary vote on 25 October in which he seeks the premiership.
body: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announced his resignation on Sunday, months before his second and final term was due to end. His Serbian Progressive Party has nominated him for prime minister ahead of snap parliamentary elections on 25 October. Parliament speaker Ana Brnabic becomes acting president, and a presidential election must be held within 90 days.

Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade. His government has faced mass protests since a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The student-led anti-corruption movement is contesting the election, and recent polls suggest it could pose a serious challenge.
more.why: Serbia balances EU membership hopes against ties with Russia and China, so its leadership shapes stability in the Western Balkans.

more.headline: France's far right wins its first Senate group
more.dek: Marine Le Pen's National Rally and allies won a record 14 seats in indirect Senate elections, enough to form a formal caucus.
body: The National Rally and its allies won at least 14 seats in France's 348-seat Senate in Sunday's indirect elections, roughly four times their previous number and enough to form a parliamentary group for the first time. Group status brings more speaking time, staff funding and the power to set up inquiries. Marine Le Pen called it a historic victory.

Senators are chosen by local elected officials, a system that favours traditional parties. The centre-right Republicans remained the largest force with at least 127 seats, and party president Bruno Retailleau was re-elected. Jordan Bardella said the RN senators would ally with the UDR. Le Pen leads polls for next year's presidential election.
more.why: The far right's advance into France's upper house is another sign of its growing strength ahead of the 2027 presidential race in the EU's second-largest economy.
